❓ Morning Boost | Leaders · Monday

Ask one team member what kind of feedback actually helps them grow.

Not everyone hears feedback the same way, and assuming they do can make it land wrong.
Ask directly in your next 1:1, notice how they've responded to past feedback, or simply ask what's been useful before.
I will ask one person how they prefer to receive feedback.
Affirmation: "Good feedback meets the person where they are."

Notice if you've been avoiding a growth conversation because it feels awkward.

Awkwardness is usually a sign the conversation matters, not a reason to skip it.

📖 Morning Boost | Employers/HR · Tuesday

Check whether one recent policy is actually understood the way it was intended.

A policy that made sense when it was written can still be misunderstood by the people it affects.
Ask a few employees to explain it in their own words, clarify where it's misunderstood, or simply rewrite the confusing part.
I will check how one policy is actually being understood today.
Affirmation: "A policy nobody understands correctly isn't really working, no matter how well it was written."

Check in on how a recent difficult conversation is sitting with the person on the other end.

A hard conversation delivered clearly in the moment can still leave someone unsettled afterward.
Follow up briefly to check how they're doing, offer space for follow-up questions, or simply confirm they know the door's still open.
I will follow up on one difficult conversation from earlier today.
Affirmation: "Clarity delivered once doesn't mean the conversation is fully closed."

Most resume advice is optimizing for the wrong reader.

Career coaches love telling you to add more keywords and quantify every bullet. But a resume's first reader is often a person, not an ATS, and people respond to clarity and a clear story before they respond to keyword density. Optimize for the human skimming it in six seconds, then worry about the algorithm.

What's the most useless resume advice you've been given?

💼 Morning Boost | Job Seekers · Thursday

Choose and prepare exactly what you'll wear and bring to your next interview, today.

Small logistics left for the last minute add stress that has nothing to do with your actual qualifications.
Lay out an outfit now, print or save your resume and notes, or map your route or test your video setup.
Today I will handle one logistical detail so future-me isn't scrambling.
Affirmation: "Taking care of the small things frees me to focus on the real conversation."

Other people's real interview experiences are often more useful than generic prep articles.
Message a former colleague, post in a relevant community, or ask someone in your network directly.

Is this the right offer, and am I set up to make an impact from day one?

Most people accept the first offer out of relief after a long search. Impact builds the muscle to pause, research, and ask, calmly and specifically, then evaluate the whole offer, not just base salary. The phase ends when you start the new role positioned to deliver.

Your goal for this phase: Have a researched target range, a rehearsed ask, and a full-offer evaluation before accepting, then a first-90-days plan for a strong start.

Can you say your ask out loud, exactly how you'd say it to them?

Watch out for: Accepting the first offer out of fear the ask will cost you the job. A reasonable, well-researched ask essentially never rescinds an offer.

You're ready to move on when: You've said your ask out loud before the real conversation, evaluated the full offer, and drafted your first-90-days plan.

🎯 A moment from this week:

The takeaway: When the volume is that high, what moves you to the top isn't luck. It's clear availability stated up front, an updated resume, and replying quickly when a recruiter reaches out.

🎯 Morning Boost | Job Seekers · Sunday

Identify the exact question you're most nervous about being asked in your next interview.

Vague anxiety about interviews in general is harder to prepare for than one specific, named fear.
Write the question down, look up how strong candidates typically answer it, or ask a friend to fire it at you cold.
Today I will write down the one question I'm most afraid of and draft a first-pass answer.
Affirmation: "Naming the fear is the first step to being ready for it."

Check whether you actually practiced out loud today, or just planned to.

Rehearsing silently in your head feels like preparation but doesn't build the same muscle as speaking.
Say one answer out loud right now, record a 60-second answer on your phone, or practice with someone this evening.
I will say one full answer out loud before the day ends.
Affirmation: "Preparation counts when it's spoken, not just thought."
